<!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows, graded by topic, for pitching an explanation or an ask at him, with each line's evidence in PROFILE-sources.md beside it. -->

# What Pavol knows

A topic reads `topic — level — how to pitch it`. `1 → 3` is a level that rose: pitch at the later one.

- 4, expert: hands-on depth; talk as to a peer.
- 3, working: uses it correctly; no explanation, define only the project's own terms.
- 2, familiar: knows the idea, not the details; a one-line reminder before it is used.
- 1, heard of: knows the name; explain it with one concrete case before using it.
- 0, new: explain from the ground up, concrete cases first, with the shortest grounding that worked where there is one.

## Topics

### Languages and tools

- Benchmarking and measurement statistics — 4 — talk as to a peer; frame speed results this way.
- Swift as a library and benchmark writer — 3 — his first frame; its compiler's insides, and its names for unique references and copy-on-write, are 1.
- Scala (2.8 era), Java and the JVM, Python, iOS, as a user — 3 — take as known; their compilers' insides are new.
- Rust, Julia, Kotlin, Clojure, C++ templates — 2 — one line on the peer's idea; Clojure's multimethods are 1.
- What generators cost against a loop — 3 — he measured it himself; use it for big operators.
- APL — 0 — the side quest is closed.

### Types and language design

- Type theory, formally — 0 — a concrete Fortress program and several cases before any rule.
- Dispatch on all arguments; exclusions; coercion against subtyping; `Any` against `Object` — 1 → 3 — take as known.
- The checker's overload rules — 1 — the idea stuck, the rules didn't; show concrete pairs of declarations.
- Erased against kept generics; traits that give behavior; a subtype with its own operation — 3 — he judges by ergonomics and reuse, not purity.
- `where` clauses; soundness — 0 → 2 — remind him that `where` narrows where a declaration applies.
- `nat` size parameters — 0 → 2 — remind him that a `nat` is a size the type carries; arithmetic on sizes is 0.
- An interface against a trait — 1 — he is unsure of the words; say "extends".

### Mathematics

- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.
- Identity elements on each type's algebra — 3 — take as known.
- Q, Z and N; `ZZ` signed, `NN` not — 0 → 3 — take as known.
- The library's number types — 2 — bottom up, `ZZ32` first; top down failed.
- Floating point — 2 — he knows IEEE rounding against Java's; infinities among the rationals were new.
- Reshape, ravel, outer product, tensor — 0 — define each on a small array.
- Mathematical notation — 1 — set it beside the Fortress code that computes it.

### Machine learning

- micrograd, microGPT, nanoGPT; FP32; integer tokens — 3 — take as known; microGPT's baseline is CPython or NumPy.
- KV cache, loss curves, early stopping, Chinchilla — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- Backpropagation, functional or tape-style, and its cost — 1 — his views are guesses.
- Big operators as ML papers write them — 1 — "hardly a yardstick", he says.
- Attention and softmax — 0 — learning them was microGPT's point for him; teach from C4's code.

### Fortress, its sources and the record

- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.
- Where intent lives: the papers, the TeX not the PDF, the team's later word, the library among the sources — 3 — his rules.
- Who did what: Ryu's front end, Park's POPL 2019 paper — 3 — take as known.
- The library's shape: `Vector` and `Matrix` for numbers only — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The specification, the papers, the library's text — 1 — unread; quote the line that decides.
- Reading Fortress code — 1 → 2 — he reads a declaration line by line; gloss each new construct.
- `label` and `exit`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `thrower`, `reflect`, DSL blocks, where whitespace counts — 0 — one concrete case each.
- FACTS, POSITIONS, the original protocol — 0 — never read; say what an entry says.
- Walk against the compiled path; the compiler's prelude — 0 → 3 — take as known.

### Compilers and run times

- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.

### The repository and the process

- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.
- The project's own terms; his past rulings — 2 — he forgets them after a gap; restate them by content.
- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.

## How to explain to him

- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
- Define each term where it is used.
- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.

## Words to avoid

- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.

## Open contradictions

- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.

content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

27	
28	**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. 30	**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. 32	**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. 58	- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);

64	
65	- values of different types are never equivalent;
66	- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
67	- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;

76	- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
77	- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);

82	**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
83	
84	- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
85	- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.

87	The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension without its condition (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.

89	**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. 91	**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. 94	
95	**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** In the interpreter's library, seven are value objects (P-178): `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64`. `QQ` is a trait, and its values are the value object `Ratio` (P-166). The compiler's prelude declares no `QQ`, and still declares the other seven as traits that a type can extend (row 1003). So the checker accepts such an object, and the object dies when its class loads (row 866). The record calls this design route A, and still calls the number types "the tower", though they do not nest.
96	
97	**The team's `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` do not exist.** No library declares them. On both paths, each is undefined as a type: 'Float is undefined.' As a `typecase` arm, each takes every value, without a message (row 959). So an arm at `Int`, copied from a team test or an old note, also takes an `RR64` and a string. In their place, write `ZZ32` for `Int`, `ZZ64` for `Long`, `RR64` for `Float`, `ZZ` for `BigNum` and `NN64` for `UnsignedLong`.
98	
99	**A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` with a radix point (P-174). Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: `n` the digit count, `m` the count of digits after the point, `r` the radix, and `v` the digits read as one integer in that radix, so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Both lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. The compiler's prelude follows the same design (P-37).

101	A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. 103	Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. 105	Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches the type as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. 106	
107	**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one exact constant, which converts as a numeral does at one of the eight number types, or takes its default. A quotient that is not whole stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. Except for a negated numeral, as `-3` above, a program's own type takes the constant only through a coercion from its default type, since coercions do not chain (P-174). So `h: Half = 10/20` needs `coerce(q: QQ)`; a numeral coercion is not enough. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
108	
109	**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). The rule converts at a declared return type too, but walk does not (row 387). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". If one of them takes the call's numerals at their default, it runs instead: `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` is `RR64`'s product, not `QQ`'s.
110	
111	**A numeral can run a more specific declaration than the one that fits its default type (P-46).** On both paths, a call with a numeral runs the declaration that fits the numeral's default type, unless the numeral's coercion reaches another declaration whose declared parameter types are strict subtypes of the first one's. Then the other runs. So `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`, but `f(1.5)` runs `f(x: RR64)` beside `f(x: RR32)`. Two departures:
112	
113	- under walk, a numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, as `a = 0` for `a: Any` (row 1016);
114	- on both paths, `g(5)` runs `g[\T\](x: T)` beside `g(x: NN32)`, where the rule gives `g(x: NN32)` (row 1017).
115	
116	**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
117	
118	**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types declares its own functional method `asFloat(self): RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. A numeral reaches a number type's own `=` by its coercion (P-46). So on both paths `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true` and `u =/= 0` is `false` for a zero `u: NN32`, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead.
119	
120	**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
121	
122	**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
123	
124	## Reductions and comprehensions
125	
126	A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
127	
128	**Where a reduction's bound names its parameter, as for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, the two paths fix an unwritten static argument from different places.** The argument is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, and the body's type only where there is no expected type or it does not fit the reduction's bound. So `x: RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` sums `ZZ32` elements in `RR64`, not in the body's type. A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types; if it is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1".
129	
130	At a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment, the checker reads the declared type, so the two paths sum in different types (row 1008): `meth(): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#4] huge(j)` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk only. Write the argument there in a program for both paths. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one. So as a call's argument, a reduction sums in its body's type on both paths. Write both arguments of `BIG MIN_MAX`, the element types of its pairs, as `BIG MIN_MAX[\ZZ32, ZZ32\][j <- 0#3] pr(j)`: the checker infers only a single static parameter (row 1007). Departures under walk:
131	
132	- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
133	- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
134	- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
135	
136	**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
137	
138	## Implementation limits
139	
140	**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). Besides a `Boolean`, walk takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition.
141	
142	**Write every parameter type.** The compiled checker refuses a parameter without a type, "Missing parameter type for", unless the exported api's declaration gives the type. Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.
143

<!-- What the transaction checks cost on the compiled path, measured 2026-10-08 by a delegated worker for the coordinator. Compiled path only; no walk timing. Nothing tracked outside this directory was changed: the checks were removed by a class-path shadow built from inATransaction-false.patch. Command: run.sh beside this file. -->

# What the transaction checks cost on the compiled path

Compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a `MutableFValue` cell. Before each read and each write of the cell, the generated code calls `BaseTask.inATransaction()`. For a local this is in `compiler/codegen/VarCodeGen.java:483-546`, for a field in `:620-726`. This note measures what share of a compiled loop's time these calls take today.

## 1. The answer

Each loop was timed in fresh JVMs, as a pair:
- "with checks" is the tree as it is;
- "without" has the checks removed by a shadow (§ 2).

How to read the table:
- Times are nanoseconds per loop iteration, or per element for TxArray.
- Each time is the median of 15 runs per variant, with the range (min-max) in brackets.
- "Pairs" is the difference inside each pair of runs, taken one after the other.
- All figures are for the third timed loop in each JVM, after the JIT's warm-up.

| program | with checks | without | difference | pairs | share | checks per iteration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TxScalar, the scalar loop | 20.42 (19.28-22.21) | 18.67 (16.42-19.99) | 1.75 | 1.96 (0.11-3.99) | 9 % | 2 |
| TxArray, the array loop | 23.17 (22.07-25.38) | 8.39 (8.17-9.05) | 14.79 | 14.60 (13.75-16.81) | 64 % | 7 |
| TxCell, the bare cell | 17.42 (16.30-19.04) | 14.56 (13.73-19.20) | 2.86 | 2.67 (-2.23-4.63) | 16 % | 2 |

- In the array loop, the checks take about two thirds of the time. Without them the loop runs 2.8 times as fast. The difference is far above the noise: every pair differs by 13.75 ns or more.
- In the scalar loop, the checks take about a tenth of the time. That difference is about as large as the spread between runs.
- One check costs about 2 ns in the array loop (14.79 / 7), and about 1 to 1.5 ns in the two scalar loops.
- The second timed loop shows the same:
  - TxScalar: 22.54 against 20.80 (1.74 ns, 8 %).
  - TxArray: 23.26 against 9.49 (13.77 ns, 59 %).
  - TxCell: 18.55 against 16.48 (2.07 ns, 11 %).
- The first timed loop includes the JIT's warm-up, as the earlier readings' single loops did:
  - TxScalar: 38.40 against 36.02 (2.39 ns, 6 %).
  - TxArray: 26.13 against 12.78 (13.35 ns, 51 %).
  - TxCell: 34.30 against 31.23 (3.07 ns, 9 %).
- Two earlier sessions of the same script, on the same day, agree (third loop; the first session had 7 runs per variant, the second 15):
  - TxScalar: 2.42 ns (11 %) and 3.08 ns (15 %).
  - TxArray: 14.15 ns (63 %) and 14.37 ns (63 %).
  - TxCell: 2.86 ns (16 %) and 3.17 ns (18 %).
- So the scalar loop's share lies between about 9 % and 15 %.

The programs, all in this directory:
- `TxScalar.fss` is the loop of `perf-probes/boxing/bench1t.fss`, which was removed in `fc89ee7a5`.
  - It runs 20 M iterations of `acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001` over `RR64`, through `for i <- seq(1#20000000)`.
  - The accumulator is a mutable local. The loop's body, a closure, reads and writes it.
- `TxArray.fss` is the hot loop of `perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` § 3 (`size-cost/SizedSum.fss`, removed in `fc89ee7a5`), without the size.
  - It uses that file's control method `sumN`. `sumN` sums an eight-element `ZZ32Vector` with a `while` loop over the mutable locals `acc` and `i`.
  - A `while` loop over two more mutable locals calls it 10 M times per round.
- `TxCell.fss` is the second rung of the boxing probe's ladder (`bench1b.fss`): TxScalar's loop with the body `acc := acc`. It shows the checks against the cell alone.

Each program runs its loop three times in one JVM, and prints each loop's result and time.

Checks per iteration, read from `javap -c` of the compiled jars (`run.sh` prints the static count for each method):
- TxScalar and TxCell make 2: one before the read of `acc` and one before the write, in the body's `apply`. The library's sequential loop (`countedseqloop`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:373-381`) has no mutable variable, so it adds no check.
- TxArray makes 7 per element:
  - 6 inside `sumN`'s loop: three reads of `i`, a read and a write of `acc`, and a write of `i`;
  - 3 per call of `sumN`: two initial writes and the final read;
  - 5 per call in the caller's loop: `k` read twice and written once, `total` read and written;
  - that is 6 + 8/8 = 7 per element.

## 2. What the shadow removed

- `inATransaction-false.patch` changes one method of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`: `inATransaction()` returns `false` without looking.
- The removed body:
  - `Thread.currentThread()`;
  - a cast to `FortressTaskRunner`;
  - a read of the `debug` flag, which is a non-final static `Boolean`;
  - two calls of `getTask()`;
  - a read of the task's `transaction` field.
- `run.sh` compiles the patched copy into `tmp/tx-probe/shadow-classes/`. It puts that directory first on the class path of the shadow variant's `java` command. Otherwise the two variants run the same command and the same compiled jars.
- The shadow leaves `MutableFValue` as it is, because the check is not there: the generated code makes the call itself, before `getValue` and `setValue`. So both variants keep:
  - the cell, with its `volatile` field, its allocation and its casts;
  - the generated bytecode. Each call site keeps its `invokestatic`, its `ifeq` and the transactional branch. The JIT folds them away once the call returns a constant.
- The shadow is correct for these programs. None of them runs `atomic`, so no transaction is ever open, and the tree's method also returns `false` on every call.
- Which method ran:
  - The JVM's class-load log cannot show it. The Fortress class loader defines `BaseTask` itself, from the bytes that `getResourceAsStream` finds first on the class path (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:141-160`).
  - The JIT's log does show it: `BaseTask::inATransaction (59 bytes)` with the checks, `(2 bytes)` without.
- The results printed the same in all 306 timed runs and all warm-up runs of the reported session:
  - TxScalar `0.8646647302294265`, the value that the boxing probe and rung 0 printed;
  - TxCell `0.5`;
  - TxArray `80000000`.

## 3. The machine

- The reported session ran on 2026-10-08, from 20:19:59 to 20:26:16 UTC.
- Tree `8f0bc7389`, on branch `tx-probe` cut from `main`. It was built in its own worktree with `ant compileAll`, then the library order.
- `nproc` 4.
- CPU "Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz", family 6, model 207, at 2100.000 MHz on all four cores.
- Load at the start: 0.36, 0.90 and 1.21 (1, 5 and 15 minutes).
- Load during the timed runs: 0.98 to 1.70, which is the measured JVM itself. A check during the second session found no other Java process.
- JDK: OpenJDK Runtime Environment, build 25.0.4.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu.
- `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. `JAVA_FLAGS`: `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`.

## 4. Against the earlier readings, and what row 302's fix changed

- **The boxing probe.** `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` § 2 charged this scalar loop's two checks 3.13 s of 9.34 s, in a Java model. That is about 156 ns per iteration, 34 % of the loop.
  - Today the same loop, compiled from Fortress, pays 1.75 ns per iteration for them: 9 % of the loop. In the first timed loop it pays 2.39 ns, 6 %.
  - So the cost per check fell from about 78 ns to about 1 ns.
- **Row 302's fix.** The fix (`53362cb88`; FACTS, "The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed") made the check read the `debug` flag before it builds its message. Before the fix, the message was built on every call.
  - `explorations/compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings", measured that fix on `bench1h`.
  - What the fix left is the body listed in § 2. In the hot loops the JIT inlines that body: `-XX:+PrintInlining` shows `inATransaction (59 bytes) inline (hot)` there.
- **The size-cost note.** `perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` § 3 found about 31 ns per element in the sized sum, with six checks per iteration in its loop, and did not split that time. It was measured on 2026-09-24, after row 302's fix.
  - TxArray is that loop's control without the size. Today it takes 23.17 ns per element, and the checks are 14.79 ns of that, 64 %.
  - The loop's six checks are the six that the note counted. With the method's entry and exit and the caller's loop, there are seven per element.
  - The 31 ns and the 23 ns come from different sessions, stacks and rounds: the size-cost stack carried the size patches, and its figure is its second round. The container's speed also varies between sessions (rung 0's report, "Two cautions"). So the two numbers do not show a change in the tree.
- **Why the array loop pays a larger share.** Its 7 checks per element sit against 8.39 ns of other work. The scalar loop's 2 checks sit against about 18.7 ns of other work: the closure call, the generator's step, two literals and two arithmetic calls.

## 5. What this measurement does not show

- **Four threads.** Every timing ran at `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`.
- **Code inside `atomic`.** No transaction is open in these programs. Inside one, a read or a write goes through `Transaction.TXRead` or `TXWrite`, and that cost is not measured. The shadow would be wrong there.
- **A top-level `var`.** Its cell lives in a static field (`VarCodeGen.java:620-726`, since `42d51c474`). None of the programs has one.
- **Other programs, microGPT among them.** The share depends on how many reads and writes of mutable variables a loop makes per unit of other work. In these three loops it runs from 9 % to 64 %.
- **Removing the checks at compile time.** The shadow removes only their run time. The generated methods keep their size: `sumN♙` stays at 319 bytes of bytecode.
- **The mechanism in machine code.** No JIT assembly was read. Two JIT controls ran on TxArray, 3 runs per variant each (third loop):
  - With `-XX:InlineSmallCode=6000`: 22.82 against 8.44 ns, a difference of 14.38 ns, the same as without the flag.
    - In one diagnostic run outside the reported session, C2 refused to inline `sumN♙` into its caller when the tree's checks were in place ("already compiled into a big method"). With the shadow it inlined the method.
    - The flag lifts that limit, and the difference does not change.
    - The reported session's own diagnostic step does not show the refusal, so this decision varies between runs.
  - With `-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis`: 43.51 against 32.67 ns, a difference of 10.84 ns. So about 11 of the 15 ns remain without escape analysis, and about 4 ns appear only with it. The reason was not examined.
- **The noise in the scalar loops.** For TxScalar and TxCell the difference is about as large as the spread between runs. Some pairs in TxCell, and in the first loops, show a negative difference. Only the medians over 15 runs, and their agreement across three sessions, support those two figures.

## Decisions

- **The shadow's scope.** I shadowed only `inATransaction()` and left `MutableFValue` as it is.
  - The alternative was to shadow `MutableFValue`'s read and write as well. That would have removed nothing more: the check is not in `MutableFValue` (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`), because the generated code makes it (`VarCodeGen.java:483-546`).
  - No decision of the curator covers this.
- **The array program.** I used `SizedSum.fss`'s control method `sumN`, without the size, rather than the sized `sumS`.
  - Reading a size as a value needs the size probes' shadow stack (`size-cost.md` § 1).
  - That note found `sumS` and `sumN` to be within noise of each other (§ 3).
- **The third program.** I added TxCell (`acc := acc`). It shows the checks against the cell alone. The boxing probe's Fortress ladder had charged them together with the cell.
- **The headline round.** I report the third timed loop in each JVM, after the JIT's warm-up. I give the first loop as well, because the earlier readings timed one loop per JVM.

## Files

- `TxScalar.fss`, `TxArray.fss` and `TxCell.fss`: the probe programs.
- `inATransaction-false.patch`: the shadow, as a patch against the tracked `BaseTask.java`.
- `run.sh`, in order:
  - it compiles the shadow and the programs;
  - it prints the machine line, the method each variant runs, the checks per method and the inlining decisions;
  - it runs one warm-up pair, then the timed runs and the JIT controls;
  - it prints the summary.
- `run.sh 15 3` produced the figures above in about six minutes. It writes only under the tree's `tmp/tx-probe/`, plus the programs' jars in the tree's bytecode cache.
=== TxArray
component TxArray
export Executable
(* Program 2 of REPORT.md: the hot loop of perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md,
   section 3 (size-cost/SizedSum.fss, removed in fc89ee7a5), without the size.
   An object makes its own eight-element ZZ32Vector; its method sums the
   elements with a while loop over two mutable locals, `acc` and `i`, bounded
   by the vector's length read at run time (SizedSum's control, sumN).  The
   method is called ten million times per round from a while loop over two
   more mutable locals, three rounds in one JVM.  The calls are resolved by
   the checker; no dispatcher runs. *)
object Vec()
  data: ZZ32Vector = makeZZ32Vector(8).fill(1)
  sumN(): ZZ32 = do
    acc: ZZ32 := 0
    i: ZZ32 := 0
    n: ZZ32 = |data|
    while i < n do
      acc += data[i]
      i += 1
    end
    acc
  end
end
round(v: Vec, r: ZZ32): () = do
  total: ZZ32 := 0
  k: ZZ32 := 0
  t0: RR64 = nanoTime()
  while k < 10000000 do
    total += v.sumN()
    k += 1
  end
  t1: RR64 = nanoTime()
  println("TxArray round " || r || " result " || total || " loop_ns " || (t1 - t0))
end
run() = do
  v: Vec = Vec()
  round(v, 1)

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
- P-175 **On the compiled path a call's arguments run in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as a tuple's elements do, so a reduction's two halves run in parallel; the one library's parallel range stops its split at a grain size, not at single elements.** The one library's range joins a reduction's halves as the arguments of one call, `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, and split down to single elements when the curator decided (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1312-1350`); the code generator evaluated a call's arguments in order, under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???", so every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of microGPT would have run its bodies one at a time once compiled programs ran the one library. The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path did not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joined on the normal path only; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1); F-350 gives what it does now. The library binding the halves as a tuple, and reductions left in sequence, are declined. Why: the specification evaluates each argument of a call in an implicit thread of its own (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:60-6
- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the team's `LexicographicOrder` computes `CMP` on its elements as a total comparison, which only totally ordered elements give (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1735-1741`), and the team's `List` extended it at every element type (`a874948ac:Library/List.fsi:67`); conditional extension, a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151), reconciles the two. Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.
- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).

1	%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
     2	%   Copyright 2009, Oracle and/or its affiliates.
     3	%   All rights reserved.
     4	%

     6	%   Use is subject to license terms.
     7	%

     9	%
    10	%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
    11	
    12	\section{Threads and Parallelism}
    13	\seclabel{threads-parallelism}
    14	
    15	\note{Reduction variables and deferred exceptions are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	\note{Thread fairness guarantee (Jan's email titled ``Re: Clarifying fairness guarantees'' sent on 14 Mar 2007)}
    18	
    19	\note{Fix citations:
    20	
    21	Victor's email titled ``Re: Fortress 1.0 spec (revision 4793)'' sent on
    22	31 Mar 2008}
    23	
    24	There are two kinds of threads in Fortress:
    25	\emph{implicit} threads and \emph{spawned}  (or \emph{explicit}) threads.
    26	Spawned threads are objects created by the \KWD{spawn} construct,
    27	described in \secref{spawn}.
    28	
    29	A thread may be in one of five states: \emph{not started},
    30	\emph{executing}, \emph{suspended}, \emph{normally completed} or
    31	\emph{abruptly completed}.  We say a thread is \emph{not started}
    32	after it is created but before it has taken a step.  This is only
    33	important for purposes of determining whether two threads are
    34	executing simultaneously; see \secref{threadlocal}.  A thread is
    35	\emph{executing} or \emph{suspended} if it has taken a step, but has
    36	not completed; see below for the distinction between executing and
    37	suspended threads.  A thread is \emph{complete} if its expression has
    38	completed evaluation.  If the expression completes normally, its value
    39	is the result of the thread.
    40	
    41	Every thread has a \emph{body} and an \emph{execution environment}.
    42	The body is an intermediate expression, which the thread evaluates in
    43	the context of the execution environment; both the body and the
    44	execution environment may change when the thread takes a step.  This
    45	environment is used to look up names in scope but bound in a block
    46	that encloses the construct that created the thread.  The execution
    47	environment of a newly created thread is the environment of the thread
    48	that created the new thread.
    49	
    50	In Fortress, a number of constructs are \emph{implicitly parallel}.
    51	An implicitly parallel construct creates a \emph{group} of one or
    52	more implicit threads.  The implicitly parallel constructs are:
    53	\begin{itemize}
    54	\item {\bf Tuple expressions:} Each element expression of the tuple
    55	  expression is evaluated in a separate implicit thread
    56	  (see \secref{tuple-expr}).
    57	\item {\bf \EXP{\KWD{also}\;\KWD{do}} blocks:} each
    58	  sub-block separated by an \KWD{also} clause is evaluated in a
    59	  separate implicit thread (see \secref{also-block}).
    60	\item {\bf Method invocations and function calls:}
    61	The receiver or the function and each of the arguments is
    62	  evaluated in a separate implicit thread
    63	  (see \secref{dotted-method-calls}, \secref{naked-method-calls},
    64	 and \secref{function-calls}).
    65	\item {\bf \KWD{for} loops, comprehensions, sums, generated
    66	    expressions, and big operators:} Parallelism in looping constructs
    67	  is specified by the generators used (see \secref{generators}).
    68	  Programmers must assume that generators that do not extend
    69	  \TYP{SequentialGenerator} can execute each iteration of the body
    70	  expression in a separate implicit thread.  The functional method
    71	  \VAR{seq} and the equivalent function \VAR{sequential} can be used
    72	  to turn any \TYP{Generator} into a \TYP{SequentialGenerator}.
    73	\item {\bf Extremum expressions:} Each guarding expression of the extremum
    74	  expression is evaluated in a separate implicit thread
    75	  (see \secref{extremum-expr}).
    76	\item {\bf Tests:}
    77	Each test is evaluated in a separate implicit thread
    78	(see \chapref{tests}).
    79	
    80	\end{itemize}
    81	
    82	Implicit threads run fork-join style:
    83	all threads in a group are created together,
    84	and they all must complete before the group as a whole completes.
    85	There is no way for a programmer to single out an implicit
    86	thread and operate upon it in any way; they are managed purely by the
    87	compiler, runtime, and libraries of the Fortress implementation.
    88	Implicit threads need not be scheduled fairly; indeed, a Fortress
    89	implementation may choose to serialize portions of any group of
    90	implicit threads, interleaving their operations in any way it likes.
    91	For example, the following code fragment may loop forever:
    92	\note{The TYP{Thread} example is commented out.}
    93	%% \input{\home/basic/examples/Eval.Thread.tex}
    94	
    95	If any implicit thread in a group completes abruptly, the group as a
    96	whole will complete abruptly as well.  Every thread in the group will
    97	either not run at all, complete (normally or abruptly), or may be
    98	terminated early as described in \secref{early-termination}.
    99	The result of the abrupt completion of the group is
   100	the result of one of the constituent threads that completes abruptly.
   101	After abrupt completion of a group of implicit threads, each reduction
   102	variable (see \secref{reduction-vars})
   103	may reflect an arbitrary subset of updates performed by the
   104	threads in the group.  This means in general that reduction variables
   105	should not be accessed after abrupt completion.  The exact behavior of reduction variables depends on the supporting generator structure and is described in \secref{defining-generators}.
   106	
   107	Spawned thread objects are reference objects of type
   108	\EXP{\TYP{Thread}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}, where
   109	\VAR{T} is the static type of the expression spawned;
   110	this trait has the following methods, each taking no arguments:
   111	\begin{itemize}
   112	\item The \VAR{val} method returns the value computed by the
   113	  subexpression of the \KWD{spawn} expression.  If the thread has not
   114	  yet completed execution, the invocation of \VAR{val} blocks until it
   115	 has done so.
   116	 A spawned thread is not permitted to exit (discussed
   117	 in \secref{label-expr}) to a surrounding label (the label is
   118	 considered to be out of scope), but may fail to catch an exception
   119	 and thus complete abruptly.
   120	 When this happens, the exception is
   121	 \emph{deferred}.  Any invocation of the \VAR{val} method on the
   122	 spawned thread throws the deferred exception.  If the spawned thread
   123	 object is discarded, the exception will be silently ignored.  In
   124	 particular, if the result of a \KWD{spawn} expression is dropped, it
   125	 is impossible to detect completion of the spawned thread or to
   126	 recover from any deferred exceptions.
   127	\item The \VAR{wait} method waits for a thread to complete,
   128	but does not return a value and will not throw a deferred exception.
   129	\item The \VAR{ready} method returns \VAR{true} if a thread
   130	has completed, and returns \VAR{false} otherwise.
   131	\item The \VAR{stop} method attempts to terminate a thread
   132	as described in \secref{early-termination}.
   133	\end{itemize}
   134	
   135	We say a spawned thread has been \emph{observed to complete} after
   136	invoking the \VAR{val} or \VAR{wait} methods, or when an invocation of
   137	the \VAR{ready} method returns \VAR{true}.
   138	
   139	In the absence of sufficient parallel resources, an attempt is made to
   140	run the subexpression of the \KWD{spawn} expression before continuing
   141	succeeding evaluation.  We can imagine that
   142	it is actually the \emph{rest} of
   143	the evaluation \emph{after} the parallel block which is spawned off
   144	in parallel.  This is a subtle technical point, but makes the
   145	sequential execution of parallel code simpler to understand, and
   146	avoids subtle problems with the asymptotic stack usage of parallel
   147	code~\cite{lazyTask,LazyThreads}.
   148	
   149	\label{abort-thread}
   150	There are three
   151	ways in which a thread can be suspended.  First, a
   152	thread that begins evaluating an implicitly parallel construct,
   153	creating a thread group, is suspended until that thread group has
   154	completed.  Second, a thread that invokes \VAR{val} or \VAR{wait} is
   155	suspended until the spawned thread completes.
   156	Finally, invoking the
   157	\VAR{abort} function from within an \KWD{atomic} expression may cause
   158	a thread to suspend; see \secref{transactions}.
   159	
   160	Threads in a Fortress program can perform operations simultaneously on
   161	shared objects.  In order to synchronize data accesses, Fortress
   162	provides \KWD{atomic} expressions (see \secref{atomic}).
   163	\chapref{memory-model} describes the memory model which is obeyed by
   164	Fortress programs.
   165	
   166	\input{\home/basic/evaluation/reduction}
   167	
   168	\input{\home/basic/evaluation/slack}
