11	
    12	\section{Abortable Atomicity}
    13	\seclabel{transactions}
    14	
    15	Fortress provides a user-level \EXP{\VAR{abort}()} function which
    16	abandons execution of the innermost \KWD{atomic} expression and rolls back its
    17	changes, requiring the \KWD{atomic} expression to execute again from
    18	the beginning.  This permits an atomic section to perform consistency
    19	checks as it runs.
    20	Invoking the \VAR{abort} function not within an \KWD{atomic} expression has
    21	no effect.
    22	The functionality provided by
    23	\EXP{\VAR{abort}()} can be abused; it is possible to induce deadlock
    24	or livelock by creating an atomic section that always fails.  Here is
    25	a simple example of a program using \EXP{\VAR{abort}()} which is
    26	incorrect because Fortress does not guarantee that the two implicit
    27	threads (created by evaluating the two elements of the tuple) will
    28	always run in parallel; it is possible for the first element of the
    29	tuple to continually abort without ever running the second element of
    30	the tuple:
    31	\note{The example is commented out because it is not yet supported nor run by the interpreter.}
    32	%% \input{\home/advanced/examples/Parallel.Abort.a.tex}
    33	
    34	Fortress also includes a \KWD{tryatomic} expression, which attempts to
    35	run its body expression atomically.  If it succeeds, the result is returned;
    36	if it aborts due to a call to \VAR{abort} or due to conflict
    37	(as described in \secref{atomic}),
    38	the checked exception \TYP{TryAtomicFailure} is thrown.  In addition, \KWD{tryatomic} is permitted to throw \TYP{TryAtomicFailure} in the absence of conflict; however, it is not permitted to fail unless some other thread performs an access to shared state while the body is being run.
    39	Conceptually \KWD{atomic} can be defined in terms of \KWD{tryatomic} as follows:
    40	\input{\home/advanced/examples/Parallel.Abort.b.tex}
    41	Unlike the above definition, an implementation may choose to suspend a
    42	thread running an \KWD{atomic} expression which invokes \VAR{abort},
    43	re-starting it at a later time when it may be possible to make further
    44	progress.  The above definition restarts the body of the \KWD{atomic}
    45	expression immediately without suspending.

11	
    12	\section{Atomic Expressions}
    13	\seclabel{atomic}
    14	
    15	\note{Modifiers on functionals such as \KWD{atomic} and \KWD{io} are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	\begin{Grammar}
    18	\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&  \KWD{atomic} \emph{AtomicBack}\\
    19	&$|$& \KWD{tryatomic} \emph{AtomicBack} \\
    20	
    21	\emph{AtomicBack}
    22	&::=& \emph{AssignExpr}\\
    23	&$|$& \emph{OpExpr}\\
    24	&$|$& \emph{DelimitedExpr}\\
    25	
    26	\end{Grammar}
    27	
    28	As Fortress is a parallel language, an executing Fortress program consists
    29	of a set of threads (See \secref{threads-parallelism} for a discussion of
    30	parallelism in Fortress).  In multithreaded programs,
    31	it is often convenient for a thread to evaluate some expressions
    32	\emph{atomically}.  For this purpose, Fortress provides \KWD{atomic}
    33	expressions.
    34	
    35	
    36	An \KWD{atomic} expression consists of \KWD{atomic}
    37	followed by a \emph{body expression}.  Evaluating an \KWD{atomic}
    38	expression is simply evaluating the body expression.  All reads and
    39	all writes which occur as part of this evaluation will appear to occur
    40	simultaneously in a single atomic step with respect to \emph{any}
    41	action performed by any thread which is dynamically outside.  This is
    42	specified in detail in \chapref{memory-model}.  The value and type of an
    43	\KWD{atomic} expression are the value and type of its body expression.
    44	
    45	A \KWD{tryatomic} expression consists of \KWD{tryatomic} followed by
    46	an expression.  It acts exactly like \KWD{atomic} except that in
    47	certain circumstances (see \secref{transactions}) it throws
    48	\TYP{TryAtomicFailure} and discards the effects of its body.
    49	
    50	A function or method with the modifier \KWD{atomic} acts as if its entire
    51	body were surrounded in an \KWD{atomic} expression.
    52	However, it is a static error if an API declares a functional \VAR{f}
    53	with the modifier \KWD{atomic} but a component implementing the API
    54	defines \VAR{f} whose body is an \KWD{atomic} expression without the
    55	modifier.  Functionals with the modifier \KWD{io} cannot be called
    56	within an \KWD{atomic} expression.  Thus, a
    57	functional must not have both \KWD{atomic} and \KWD{io} modifiers.
    58	
    59	When the body of an \KWD{atomic} expression completes abruptly, the
    60	\KWD{atomic} expression completes abruptly in the same way.  If it
    61	completes abruptly by exiting to an enclosing \KWD{label} expression,
    62	writes within the block are retained and become visible to other
    63	threads.  If it completes abruptly by throwing an uncaught exception,
    64	all writes to objects allocated before the \KWD{atomic}
    65	expression began evaluation are discarded.  Writes to newly
    66	allocated objects are retained.  Any variable reverts to the value it
    67	held before evaluation of the \KWD{atomic} expression began.  Thus, the
    68	only values retained from the abruptly completed \KWD{atomic} expression
    69	will be reachable from the exception object through a chain of newly
    70	allocated objects.
    71	
    72	Atomic expressions may be nested arbitrarily; the above semantics
    73	imply that an inner \KWD{atomic} expression is atomic with respect to
    74	evaluations which occur dynamically outside the inner \KWD{atomic}
    75	expression but dynamically inside an enclosing \KWD{atomic}.
    76	
    77	Implicit threads may be created dynamically within an \KWD{atomic}
    78	expression.  These implicit threads will complete before the
    79	\KWD{atomic} expression itself does so.  The implicit threads may
    80	run in parallel, and will see one another's writes; they may
    81	synchronize with one another using nested \KWD{atomic} expressions.
    82	
    83	Note that \KWD{atomic} expressions may be evaluated in parallel with
    84	other expressions.  An \KWD{atomic} expression experiences
    85	\emph{conflict} when another thread attempts to read or write a memory
    86	location which is accessed by the \KWD{atomic} expression.  The
    87	evaluation of such an expression must be partially serialized with the
    88	conflicting memory operation (which might be another \KWD{atomic}
    89	expression).  The exact mechanism by which this occurs will vary; the
    90	necessary serialization is provided by the implementation.  In
    91	general, the evaluation of a conflicting \KWD{atomic} expression may
    92	be abandoned, forcing the effects of execution to be discarded and
    93	execution to be retried.  The longer an \KWD{atomic} expression
    94	evaluates and the more memory it touches the greater the chance of
    95	conflict and the larger the bottleneck a conflict may impose.
    96	
    97	For example,
    98	the following code uses a shared counter atomically:
    99	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.Atomic.tex}
   100	The loop body reads \EXP{a_i} and \VAR{sum}, then adds them and
   101	writes the result back to \VAR{sum}; this will appear to occur
   102	atomically with respect to all other threads---including both other
   103	iterations of the loop body and other simultaneous calls to
   104	\VAR{accumArray}.  Note in particular that the \KWD{atomic} expression
   105	will appear atomic with respect to reads and writes of \EXP{a_i} and \VAR{sum} that do  not occur in
   106	\KWD{atomic} expressions.

11	
    12	\section{Shared and Local Data}
    13	\seclabel{threadlocal}
    14	
    15	\note{The method \VAR{copy} is not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	Every object in a Fortress program is considered to be either
    18	\emph{shared} or \emph{local} (collectively referred to as the
    19	\emph{sharedness} of the object).  A local object must be transitively
    20	reachable (through zero or more object references) from the variables
    21	of at most one running thread.  A local object may be accessed more
    22	cheaply than a shared object, particularly in the case of atomic reads
    23	and writes.  Sharedness is ordinarily managed implicitly by the
    24	Fortress implementation.
    25	Control over sharedness is intended to be a
    26	performance optimization; however, functions such as \VAR{isShared} and
    27	\VAR{localize} provided by the Fortress libraries
    28	can affect program semantics, and must be used with care.
    29	
    30	The sharedness of an object must be contrasted with its region.  The
    31	region of an object describes where that object is located on the
    32	machine.  The sharedness of an object describes whether the object is
    33	visible to one thread or to many.  A local object need not actually
    34	reside in a region near the thread to which it is visible (though
    35	ordinarily it will).
    36	
    37	The following rules govern sharedness:
    38	\begin{itemize}
    39	\item Reference objects are initially local when they are constructed.
    40	\item The sharedness of an object may change as the program executes.\footnote{Note, for example, that the present Fortress implementation immediately makes every object shared after construction, so that \VAR{isShared()} will always return \VAR{true}.}
    41	\item If an object is currently transitively reachable from more than
    42	  one running thread, it must be shared.
    43	\item When a reference to a local object is stored into a field of a
    44	  shared object, the local object must be \emph{published}: Its
    45	  sharedness is changed to shared, and all of the data to which it
    46	  refers is also published.
    47	\item The value of a local variable referenced by a thread must be
    48	  published before that thread may be run in parallel with the thread
    49	  which created it.  Values assigned to the variable while the
    50	  threads run in parallel must also be published.
    51	\item A field with value type is assigned by copying, and thus has the
    52	   sharedness of the containing object or closure.
    53	\end{itemize}
    54	
    55	Publishing can be expensive, particularly if the structure being
    56	broadcast is large and heavily nested; this can cause an apparently
    57	short \KWD{atomic} expression (a single write, say) to run arbitrarily
    58	long.  To avoid this, the library programmer can request that an
    59	object be published by calling the semantically transparent function
    60	\VAR{shared} provided by the Fortress libraries:
    61	\input{\home/advanced/examples/Parallel.Shared.a.tex}
    62	A local copy of an object can be obtained by calling \VAR{copy}, a
    63	method on trait \TYP{Any}:
    64	\note{Example is commented out because it is not yet supported nor run by the interpreter.}
    65	% %localVar := sharedVar.copy()
    66	% \begin{Fortress}
    67	% \(\VAR{localVar} \ASSIGN \VAR{sharedVar}.\VAR{copy}()\)
    68	% \end{Fortress}
    69	
    70	Two additional functions are provided which permit different choices of
    71	program behavior based on the sharedness of objects:
    72	\begin{itemize}
    73	\item The function \EXP{\VAR{isShared}(o)} returns \VAR{true} when
    74	\VAR{o} is shared, and \VAR{false} when it is local.  This permits
    75	the program to take different actions based on sharedness.
    76	\item The function \EXP{\VAR{localize}(o)} is provided that attempts to make a local version of object \VAR{o}, by copying if necessary
    77	equivalent to the following expression:
    78	\note{Example is commented out because it is not yet supported nor run by the interpreter.}
    79	%% \input{\home/advanced/examples/Parallel.Shared.b.tex}
    80	%% %% %if o.isShared then o.copy() else o end
    81	%% %% \begin{Fortress}
    82	%% %% \(\KWD{if} o.\VAR{isShared} \KWD{then} o.\VAR{copy}() \KWD{else} o \KWD{end}\)
    83	%% %% \end{Fortress}
    84	\end{itemize}
    85	These functions must be used with extreme caution.  For example,
    86	\VAR{localize} should be used only when there is a unique
    87	reference to the object being localized.  The \VAR{localize} function
    88	can have unexpected behavior if there is a reference to \VAR{o} from
    89	another local object \VAR{p}.  Updates to \VAR{o} will be visible
    90	through \VAR{p}; subsequent publication of \VAR{p} will publish
    91	\VAR{o}.  By contrast, if \VAR{o} was already shared, and referred to
    92	by another shared object, the newly-localized copy will be entirely
    93	distinct; changes to the copy will not be visible through \VAR{p}, and
    94	publishing \VAR{p} will not affect the locality of the copy.

11	
    12	\chapter{Memory Model}
    13	\chaplabel{memory-model}
    14	
    15	Fortress programs are highly multithreaded by design; the language
    16	makes it easy to expose parallelism.  However, many Fortress objects
    17	are mutable; without judicious use of synchronization
    18	constructs---reductions and \KWD{atomic} expressions---\emph{data
    19	  races} will occur and programs will behave in an unpredictable way.
    20	The memory model has two important functions:
    21	\begin{enumerate}
    22	\item Define a programming discipline for the use of data and
    23	  synchronization, and describe the behavior of programs that obey
    24	  this discipline.  This is the purpose of
    25	  \secref{programmer-memory-model}.
    26	\item Define the behavior of programs that do not obey the programming
    27	  discipline.  This constrains the optimizations that can be performed
    28	  on Fortress programs.  The remaining sections of this chapter
    29	  specify the detailed memory model that Fortress programs must obey.
    30	\end{enumerate}
    31	
    32	\section{Principles}
    33	
    34	The Fortress memory model has been written with several important
    35	guiding principles in mind.  Violations of these principles must be
    36	taken as a flaw in the memory model specification rather than an
    37	opportunity to be exploited by the programmer or implementor.  The most
    38	important principle is this: violations of the Fortress memory model
    39	must still respect the underlying data abstractions of the Fortress
    40	programming language.  All data structures must be properly
    41	initialized before they can be read by another thread, and a program
    42	must not read values that were never written.  When a program fails,
    43	it must fail gracefully by throwing an exception.
    44	
    45	The second goal is nearly as important, and much more difficult:
    46	present a memory model which can be understood thoroughly by
    47	programmers and implementors.  It must never be difficult to judge
    48	whether a particular program behavior is permitted by the model.
    49	Where possible, it must be possible to check that a program obeys
    50	the programming discipline.
    51	
    52	The final goal of the Fortress memory model is to permit aggressive
    53	optimization of Fortress programs.  A multiprocessor memory model can
    54	rule out optimizations that might be performed by a compiler for a
    55	uniprocessor.  The Fortress memory model attempts to rule out as few
    56	behaviors as possible, but more importantly attempts to make it easy
    57	to judge whether a particular optimization is permitted or not.  The
    58	semantics of Fortress already allows permissive operation reordering in
    59	many programs, simply by virtue of the implicitly parallel semantics
    60	of tuple evaluation and looping.
    61	
    62	\section{Programming Discipline}
    63	\seclabel{programmer-memory-model}
    64	
    65	If Fortress programmers obey the following discipline, they can expect
    66	sequentially consistent behavior from their Fortress programs:
    67	\begin{itemize}
    68	
    69	\item Updates to shared mutable locations must always be performed using an
    70	  \KWD{atomic} expression.  A location is considered to be shared if
    71	  and only if that location can be accessed by more than one thread at
    72	  a time.  For example, statically partitioning an array among many
    73	  threads need not make the array elements shared; only elements
    74	  actually accessed by more than one thread are considered to be
    75	  shared.
    76	
    77	\item Within a thread or group of implicit threads objects must not
    78	  be accessed through aliased references; this can yield unexpected
    79	  results.  \secref{aliasing} defines the notion of \emph{apparently
    80	    disjoint} references.  An object must not be written through one
    81	  reference when it is accessed through another apparently disjoint
    82	  reference.
    83	
    84	\end{itemize}
    85	
    86	The following stylistic guidelines reduce the possibility of
    87	pathological behavior when a program strays from the above discipline:
    88	\begin{itemize}
    89	
    90	\item Where feasible, reduction must be used in favor of updating a
    91	  single shared object.
    92	
    93	\item Immutable fields and variables must be used wherever
    94	  practical.  We discuss this further in \secref{immutability}.
    95	
    96	\item A getter or a setter should behave as though it is performing a
    97	  simple field access, even if it internally accesses many
    98	  locations.  The simplest (but not necessarily most
    99	  efficient) way to obtain the appropriate behavior is to make
   100	  hand-coded accessors \KWD{atomic}.  \secref{gettersetter} expands on
   101	  this.
   102	
   103	\end{itemize}
   104	
   105	\subsection{Immutability}
   106	\seclabel{immutability}
   107	
   108	Recall from \secref{memory-ops} that we can distinguish mutable and
   109	immutable memory locations.  Any thread that reads an immutable field
   110	will obtain the initial value written when the object was constructed.
   111	In this regard it is worth re-emphasizing the distinction between an
   112	object reference and the object it refers to.  A location that does not
   113	contain a value object contains an object reference.  If the field is
   114	immutable, that means the reference is not subject to change; however,
   115	fields of the object referred to may still be modified in accordance with the
   116	memory model.
   117	
   118	By contrast, recall that all the fields of a value object are
   119	immutable; however, a mutable location may have a value type.  Such a
   120	location can be written, completely replacing the value object it
   121	contains.  Similarly, reading the value contained in such a location
   122	conceptually causes the entire value object to be read; if this isn't
   123	followed by an immediate field reference, the read must be performed
   124	atomically.  This may potentially be expensive (see
   125	\secref{read-atomicity}).
   126	
   127	\subsection{Providing the Appearance of a Single Object}
   128	\seclabel{gettersetter}
   129	
   130	In practice, most accesses to fields occur through a mediating getter
   131	or setter method.  It should not be possible for the programmer to
   132	tell whether a given getter or setter directly accesses a field or if
   133	it performs additional computations.  Similarly, any subscripting
   134	operation must be indistinguishable from accessing a single field.
   135	Thus, accessor methods and subscripting methods should provide the
   136	appearance of atomicity, as described in \secref{read-atomicity}.
   137	\Library\ are written to preserve this abstraction.  For
   138	example, the \TYP{Array} type in Fortress makes use of one or more
   139	underlying \TYP{HeapSequence}s, and array subscripting
   140	preserves the atomicity guarantees of this underlying object.
   141	
   142	\subsection{Modifying Aliased Objects}
   143	\seclabel{aliasing}
   144	
   145	In common with Fortran, and unlike most other popular programming
   146	languages, Fortress gives special treatment to accesses to a location
   147	through different aliases.  For the purposes of variable aliasing, it
   148	is important to define the notion of \emph{apparently disjoint} (or
   149	simply disjoint) object and field references.  If two references are not
   150	disjoint, we say they are \emph{certainly the same}, or just \emph{the
   151	  same}.  By contrast, we say object references are \emph{identical}
   152	if they refer to the same object, and \emph{distinct} otherwise.
   153	Accesses to fields reached via apparently disjoint object references
   154	may be reordered (except an initializing write is never reordered with
   155	respect to other accesses to the identical location).
   156	
   157	\note{
   158	Problem: Consider a function call on a tree and its subtree.  The
   159	common subtree won't be considered disjoint, right?  We bottom out
   160	to comparing an argument to a field reference, and have recourse to
   161	the calling context.  Is that what we want, or do we want to
   162	consider them a priori distinct (I think so).
   163	}
   164	
   165	\note{
   166	Questions -- Sukyoung
   167	
   168	1. What and how do we guarantee with these?
   169	
   170	2. coverage? if or if and only if?
   171	}
   172	
   173	Distinct references are always disjoint.  Two identical
   174	references are apparently disjoint if they are obtained in any of the
   175	following ways:
   176	\begin{itemize}
   177	\item distinct parameters of a single function call
   178	\item distinct fields
   179	\item a parameter and a field
   180	\item identically named fields read from apparently disjoint object references
   181	\item distinct reads of a single location for which there may be an
   182	  interposing write
   183	\end{itemize}
   184	When comparing variables defined in different scopes, these rules will
   185	eventually lead to reads of fields or to reads of parameters in some
   186	common containing scope.
   187	
   188	We extend this to field references as follows: two field references
   189	are apparently disjoint if they refer to distinct fields, or they
   190	refer to identically named fields read from apparently disjoint object
   191	references.
   192	
   193	Consider the following example:
   194	\input{\home/basic/examples/MemModel.Aliases.f.tex}
   195	Here \VAR{x} and \VAR{y} in \VAR{f} are
   196	apparently disjoint; the writes may be reordered, so the call
   197	\EXP{f(a,a)} may assign either 17 or 32 to \EXP{a_{0}}.
   198	
   199	A similar phenomenon occurs in the following example:
   200	\input{\home/basic/examples/MemModel.Aliases.g.tex}
   201	Again \VAR{x} and \VAR{y} are apparently distinct in \VAR{g}, so the
   202	write to \EXP{x_{0}} and the read of \EXP{y_{0}} may be reordered.
   203	The call \EXP{g(a,a)} will assign 17 to \EXP{a_{0}} but may return
   204	either the initial value of \EXP{a_{0}} or 17.
   205	
   206	It is safe to \emph{read} an object through apparently disjoint references:
   207	\input{\home/basic/examples/MemModel.Aliases.h.tex}
   208	A call to \EXP{h(a,a)} will read \EXP{a_{0}} twice without ambiguity.
   209	Note, however, that the reads may still be reordered, and if
   210	\EXP{a_{0}} is written in parallel by another thread this reordering
   211	can be observed.
   212	
   213	If necessary, \KWD{atomic} expressions can be used to order disjoint field
   214	references:
   215	\input{\home/basic/examples/MemModel.Aliases.fprime.tex}
   216	Here the call \EXP{f'(a,a)} ends up setting \EXP{a_{0}} to
   217	32.  Note that simply using a single \KWD{atomic} expression
   218	containing one or both writes is not sufficient;
   219	the two writes must be in distinct \KWD{atomic} expressions
   220	to be required to occur in order.
   221	
   222	When references occur in distinct calling contexts, they are
   223	disambiguated at the point of call:
   224	\input{\home/basic/examples/MemModel.Aliases.jkl.tex}
   225	Here if we call \EXP{k(a)} the order of the writes performed by the
   226	two calls to \VAR{j} is unambiguous, and \EXP{a_{0}} is 32 in the end.
   227	By contrast, \EXP{l(a,a)} calls \VAR{j} with two apparently disjoint
   228	references, and the writes in these two calls may thus be reordered.
   229	
   230	\note{
   231	Some stuff here about overwriting.
   232	
   233	Some stuff here about nested functions and accesses to stuff in the
   234	enclosing scope.
   235	}
   236	
   237	\section{Read and Write Atomicity}
   238	\seclabel{read-atomicity}
   239	
   240	This section makes potentially very controversial choices.  In
   241	particular, the unit of atomic read/write can be considerably larger
   242	than the natural read/write granularity of the underlying machine.
   243	So we have to use hugely expensive mechanisms (the easiest of which
   244	is boxing and copying) if we read or write non-trivial objects
   245	non-transactionally.
   246	
   247	\note{I take comfort in the fact that we can obtain the required semantics
   248	by just putting these large operations into a read-only or
   249	write-only transaction and detecting/resolving conflict using the
   250	same set of underlying mechanisms.}
   251	
   252	Any read or write to a location is
   253	\emph{indivisible}.  In practical terms, this means that each read
   254	operation will see exactly the data written by a single write
   255	operation.  Note in particular that indivisibility holds for a mutable
   256	location containing a large value object.  It is convenient to imagine
   257	that every access to a mutable location is surrounded by an
   258	\KWD{atomic} expression.  However, there are a number of ordering
   259	guarantees provided by \KWD{atomic} accesses that are not respected by
   260	non-\KWD{atomic} accesses.
   261	
   262	\section{Ordering Dependencies among Operations}
   263	
   264	The Fortress memory model is specified in terms of two orderings:
   265	dynamic program order (see \chapref{evaluation} and
   266	\chapref{expressions}) and memory order.  The actual order of memory
   267	operations in a given program execution is \emph{memory order}, a
   268	total order on all memory operations.  Dynamic program order
   269	constrains memory order.  However, memory operations need not be
   270	ordered according to dynamic program order; many memory operations,
   271	even reads and writes to a single field or array element, can be
   272	reordered.  Programmers who adhere to the model in
   273	\secref{programmer-memory-model} can expect sequentially consistent
   274	behavior: the global ordering of memory operations will respect dynamic program order.
   275	
   276	Here is a summary of the salient aspects of memory order:
   277	\begin{itemize}
   278	\item There is a single memory order which is respected in all threads.
   279	\item Every read obtains the value of the immediately preceding write
   280	  to the identical location in memory order.
   281	\item Memory order on \KWD{atomic} expressions respects dynamic program order.
   282	\item Memory order respects dynamic program order for operations that
   283	  certainly access the same location.
   284	\item Initializing writes are ordered before any other memory access
   285	  to the same location.
   286	\end{itemize}
   287	
   288	\subsection{Dynamic Program Order}
   289	
   290	Much of the definition of \emph{dynamic program order} is given in the
   291	descriptions of individual expressions in \chapref{expressions}.  It
   292	is important to understand that dynamic program order represents a
   293	conceptual, naive view of the order of operations in an execution;
   294	this naive view is used to define the more permissive memory order
   295	permitted by the memory model.  Dynamic program order is a partial
   296	order, rather than a total order; in most cases operations in
   297	different threads will not be ordered with respect to one another.
   298	There is an important exception: there is an ordering dependency among
   299	threads when a thread starts or must be complete.
   300	
   301	\note{TODO: re-factor into expressions chapter.}
   302	
   303	An expression is ordered in dynamic program order after any expression
   304	it dynamically contains, with one exception: a \KWD{spawn} expression
   305	is dynamically ordered before any subexpression of its body.  The body
   306	of the \KWD{spawn} is dynamically ordered before any point at which
   307	the spawned thread object is observed to have completed.
   308	
   309	Only expressions whose evaluation completes normally
   310	occur in dynamic program order,
   311	unless the expression is ``directly responsible'' for generating
   312	abrupt termination.  Examples of the latter case are \KWD{throw} and \KWD{exit}
   313	expressions and division by zero.  In particular, when
   314	the evaluation of a
   315	subexpression of an expression completes abruptly, causing the
   316	expression itself to complete abruptly, the containing expression does
   317	not occur in dynamic program order.
   318	A \KWD{label} block is ordered
   319	after an \KWD{exit} that targets it.
   320	The expressions in a \KWD{catch}
   321	clause whose \KWD{try} block throws a matching exception are ordered
   322	after the \KWD{throw} and before any expression in the \KWD{finally}
   323	clause.  If the \KWD{catch} completes normally, the \KWD{try} block as
   324	a whole is ordered after the expressions in the \KWD{finally} clause.
   325	For this reason, when we refer to the place of non-\KWD{spawn}
   326	expression in dynamic program order, we mean the expression or any
   327	expression it dynamically contains.
   328	
   329	
   330	For any construct giving rise to implicit threads---tuple
   331	evaluation, function or method call, or the body of an expression with
   332	generators such as \KWD{for}---there is no ordering in dynamic program
   333	order between the expression executed in each thread in the group.
   334	\note{Ugh, this is bogus:}
   335	These subexpressions are ordered with respect to expressions which
   336	precede or succeed the group.
   337	
   338	When a function or method is called, the body of the function or
   339	method occurs dynamically after the arguments and function or
   340	receiver; the call expression is ordered after the body of the called
   341	function or method.
   342	
   343	For conditional expressions such as \KWD{if}, \KWD{case}, and
   344	\KWD{typecase}, the expression being tested is
   345	ordered dynamically before any chosen branch.  This branch is in turn
   346	ordered dynamically before the conditional expression itself.
   347	
   348	Iterations of the body of a \KWD{while} loop are ordered by dynamic
   349	program order.  Each evaluation of the guarding predicate is ordered
   350	after any previous iteration and before any succeeding iteration.  The
   351	\KWD{while} loop as a whole is ordered after the final evaluation of
   352	the guarding predicate, which yields \VAR{false}.
   353	
   354	An iteration of the body of a \KWD{for} loop,
   355	and each evaluation of the body expression in a comprehension or big operator,
   356	is ordered after the generator expressions.
   357	
   358	\subsection{Memory Order}
   359	
   360	\note{
   361	Question: Should variables (esp parameters and mutable locals) be
   362	considered locations which can be read from / written to?  This
   363	makes things easy to explain, but may not give the behavior we expect.}
   364	
   365	\emph{Memory order} gives a total order on all memory accesses in a
   366	program execution.  A read obtains the value of the most recent prior
   367	write to the identical location in memory order.  In this section we
   368	describe the constraints on memory order, guided by dynamic program
   369	order.  We can think of these constraints as specifying a partial
   370	order which must be respected by memory order.  The simplest constraint
   371	is that accesses certainly to the same location must respect dynamic
   372	program order.  Apparently disjoint accesses need not respect dynamic
   373	program order, but an initializing write must be ordered before all
   374	other accesses to the identical location in program order.
   375	
   376	\note{The following doesn't fully address Bill Pugh's concerns: it still
   377	allows cheesy outs where we write a bogus location which is never
   378	read.  Also, we order atomics in memory order even if they don't
   379	share common data; can we tell, and do we care}
   380	
   381	Accesses in distinct (non-nested) \KWD{atomic} expressions respect
   382	dynamic program order.  Given an \KWD{atomic} expression, we divide
   383	accesses into four classes:
   384	\begin{enumerate}
   385	\item Constituents, dynamically contained within the \KWD{atomic} expression.
   386	\item Ancestors, dynamically ordered before the \KWD{atomic} expression.
   387	\item Descendants, dynamically ordered after the \KWD{atomic} expression.
   388	\item Peers, dynamically unordered with respect to operations
   389	  dynamically contained within the \KWD{atomic} expression.
   390	\end{enumerate}
   391	We say an \KWD{atomic} expression is \emph{effective} if it contains
   392	an access to a location, there is a peer access to the identical
   393	location, and at least one of these accesses is a write.  For an
   394	effective \KWD{atomic} expression, every peer access must either be
   395	a \emph{predecessor} or a \emph{successor}.  A predecessor must occur
   396	before every constituent and every descendant in memory order.  A
   397	successor must occur after every constituent and every ancestor in
   398	memory order.  Every ancestor must occur before every descendant in
   399	memory order.
   400	
   401	The above conditions guarantee that there is a single, global ordering
   402	for the effective \KWD{atomic} expressions in a Fortress program.  This
   403	means that for any executions of \KWD{atomic} expressions $A$ and $B$ one of the
   404	following conditions holds:
   405	\begin{itemize}
   406	\item $A$ is dynamically contained inside $B$.
   407	\item $B$ is dynamically contained inside $A$.
   408	\item Every expression dynamically contained in $A$ precedes every
   409	  expression dynamically contained in $B$ in memory order.  This will
   410	  always hold when $A$ is dynamically ordered before $B$.
   411	\item Every expression dynamically contained in $B$ precedes every
   412	  expression dynamically contained in $A$ in memory order.  This will
   413	  always hold when $B$ is dynamically ordered before $A$.
   414	\end{itemize}
   415	The above rules are also sufficient to guarantee that \KWD{atomic}
   416	expressions nested inside an enclosing \KWD{atomic} behave with
   417	respect to one another just as if they had occurred at the top level
   418	in an un-nested context.
   419	
   420	Any access preceding a \KWD{spawn} in dynamic program order will
   421	precede accesses in the spawned expression in memory order.  Any
   422	access occurring after a spawned thread has been observed to
   423	complete in dynamic program order will occur after accesses in the
   424	spawned expression in memory order.
   425	
   426	A reduction variable in a \KWD{for} loop does not have a single
   427	associated location; instead, there is a distinct location for each
   428	loop iteration, initialized by writing the identity of the reduction.
   429	These locations are distinct from the location associated with the
   430	reduction variable in the surrounding scope.  In memory order there is
   431	a read of each of these locations each of which succeeds the last
   432	access to that variable in the loop iteration, along with a read of
   433	the location in the enclosing scope which succeeds all accesses to
   434	that location preceding the loop in dynamic program order.  These
   435	reads are followed by a write of the location in the enclosing scope
   436	which in turn precedes all accesses to that location that succeed the
   437	loop in dynamic program order.
   438	
   439	\note{The following is controversial.  I think this is effectively the
   440	condition the X10 guys are trying to capture formally in their
   441	memory model work.}
   442	
   443	Finally, reads and writes in Fortress programs must respect dynamic
   444	program order for operations that are \emph{semantically related}.
   445	If the read $A$ precedes the write $B$ in dynamic program order, and
   446	the value of $B$ can be determined in some fashion without recourse to
   447	$A$, then these operations are not semantically related.  A simple
   448	example is if $A$ is a reference to variable \VAR{x} and $B$ is the
   449	assignment \EXP{y \ASSIGN x \cdot 0}.  Here it can be determined that
   450	\EXP{y \ASSIGN 0} without recourse to $x$ and these variables are not
   451	semantically related.  By contrast, the write \EXP{y \ASSIGN x} is
   452	always semantically related to the read of \VAR{x}.  Note that two
   453	operations can only be semantically related if a transitive data or
   454	control dependency exists between them.

11	
    12	\section{Memory and Memory Operations}
    13	\seclabel{memory-ops}
    14	
    15	\note{Check for \emph{initializing write} is not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	In this specification,
    18	the term \emph{memory} refers to a set of abstract \emph{locations};
    19	the memory is used to model sharing and mutation.
    20	A location has an associated type,
    21	and \emph{contains} a value of that type
    22	(i.e., the type of the value is a subtype of the type of the location).
    23	Locations can have non-object trait types; by contrast, a value always has an object type.
    24	
    25	There are three operations that can be performed on memory:
    26	\emph{allocation}, \emph{read}, and \emph{write}.
    27	Reads and writes are collectively called \emph{memory accesses}.
    28	Intuitively,
    29	a read operation takes a location
    30	and returns the value contained in that location,
    31	and a write operation takes a location and a value of the location's type
    32	and changes the contents of the location
    33	so the location contains the given value.
    34	Accesses need not take place in the order in which they occur in the program text; a detailed account of memory behavior appears in \chapref{memory-model}.
    35	
    36	Allocation creates a new location of a given type.
    37	Allocation occurs when a mutable variable is declared, or when a
    38	reference object is constructed.  In the latter case, a new location
    39	is allocated for each field of the object.
    40	Abstractly, locations are never reclaimed;
    41	in practice, memory reclamation is handled by garbage collection.
    42	
    43	A freshly allocated location is \emph{uninitialized}.
    44	The type system and memory model in Fortress guarantee that an
    45	\emph{initializing write} is performed to every location if it is ever read,
    46	and that this write occurs before any read of the location.
    47	Any location whose value can be written after initialization is
    48	\emph{mutable}.  Mutable locations consist of
    49	mutable variables and mutable fields of reference objects.
    50	Any location whose value cannot be written after
    51	initialization is \emph{immutable}.
    52	Immutable locations are the non-\KWD{settable} immutable fields of a reference object.

A spawned thread is created using a \KWD{spawn} expression.  A
\KWD{spawn} expression consists of \KWD{spawn} followed by an
expression.  A \KWD{spawn} expression spawns a thread which evaluates
its subexpression in parallel with any succeeding evaluation.  The
value of a \KWD{spawn} expression is the spawned thread
and the type of the expression is \EXP{\TYP{Thread}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket},
where \VAR{T} is the static type of the expression spawned.
A \KWD{spawn} expression constitutes an \KWD{io} action, and thus cannot be run
within the body of an \KWD{atomic} expression.
A \KWD{spawn} expression cannot be run
within the body of an \KWD{atomic} expression.
The semantics of spawned threads are discussed in \secref{threads-parallelism}.
A \KWD{throws} clause does not include naked type variables.
Every element in a \KWD{throws} clause is a subtype of
\TYP{CheckedException}.
When a function declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{function definition}.
Function declarations can be mutually recursive.

Function declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{atomic}:}
A function with the modifier \KWD{atomic} acts as if its entire
body were surrounded in an \KWD{atomic} expression discussed in
\secref{atomic}.

\paragraph{\KWD{io}:}
Functions that perform externally visible input/output actions
are said to be \KWD{io} functions.
An \KWD{io} function must not be invoked from a non-\KWD{io} function.

A function takes exactly one argument, which may be a tuple.
When a function takes a tuple argument, we abuse terminology by saying that
the function takes multiple arguments.

\note{The \KWD{transient} modifier and varargs parameters are eliminated.}

\note{What does it mean to have an invariant on an object?

Christine: The easy answer is that on entrance and exit of every method the invariant is true. Unfortunately I could be in the middle of a method with the invariant violated and want to call another method.

Guy: One might argue that invariants should hold on entry and exit of methods that appear in the API. This can be approximated as: invariants must hold before and after every method that is not marked private.

Need a more concrete proposal.

Does the modifier \KWD{atomic} on a functional check its contract also?

<!-- A read-only review, 2026-11-08, of how Fortress runs code in parallel and keeps shared state safe, for Pavol's question of 2026-11-08: the fork/join pool, the two STMs and the code that joins them, on walk and on the compiled path. It has their provenance, 31 targeted programs at four threads on both paths, a cost measurement, the specification's answers, the JVM-side reading in the terms of Goetz and the Java Memory Model, microGPT's exposure, eight new defects and a rewrite of row 933 drafted in the ledger's form, and the curator's answer. Tree main at f5aa647de (the batch-28 landing); base 157323e51; nothing in the tree was changed. -->

# The foundations of Fortress's parallelism: fork/join, the two STMs, and what microGPT stands on

## 0. What was run, and on what

- **Trees.** Walk programs ran on the base build `/home/user/fortress-base28` (157323e51) through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh`, using private caches in my scratchpad. Compiled programs ran in a worktree seeded at main `f5aa647de`, with `seed-worktree.sh` then `ant compileAll` and the library order (`EXIT=0`, five jars). Every new compiled finding was also run on the base, through `old-fortress.sh … compile/run`. The worktree has been removed (`git worktree list` shows only `fortress`, `fortress-base28` and `fortress-transcripts-blinded`). `df -P /home/user` read 22 GB free at the start and at the end.
- **Where the base matters.** The base 157323e51 lacks rung A's slot API (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`, `FortressArrayStore`). This matters only for the store's init race (§7, row N7), which ran on f5aa647de alone. Walk's STM is byte-identical between the two (§2). On the base, walk's arrays reach `AtomicArray` through the old `PrimitiveArray` glue; on main they reach it through `ArrayOps`. They are the same cells (`compile-ladder/rung-array-store/REPORT.md:18`).
- **Programs.** All probe programs and scripts are under `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/parallelism/`, in `walk/`, `compiled/` and `java/probe/`, with the runners `runwalk.sh`, `runcomp.sh`, `runbase.sh` and `runcost.sh`. Every program ran three times at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4` unless stated otherwise. Every wait was under 240 s.
- **Machine, for the one timing (§3.3).** nproc 4; Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 2100 MHz; load 1.13 at the start and 1.51 at the end; OpenJDK 25.0.4.1+1-1-24.04.4; compiled path only (P-29); nothing else of mine was running.

## 1. The blocks, on each path

### 1.1 Walk: tasks and the pool (`interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`)

- **The pool.** `FortressTaskRunnerGroup` is a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool` (`FortressTaskRunnerGroup.java:16-33`, asyncMode false, so LIFO local queues). `FortressTaskRunner` is its worker thread. It holds a `volatile BaseTask task`, the "current task" through which every transaction is found (`FortressTaskRunner.java:27`, `:54-61`).
- **Tasks.** `BaseTask extends RecursiveAction` (`BaseTask.java:21`). A child copies its parent's transaction when it is constructed (`:35`). So **the implicit threads of an `atomic` block share the block's transaction object**.
- **`TupleTask`.** It is the unit for tuples, call arguments and `do … also` arms. `compute()` makes itself the current task, catches every `Exception` into `err` and nulls its transaction (`TupleTask.java:33-52`). `Evaluator.forDo` and `evalExprListParallel` save the current task, call `ForkJoinTask.invokeAll`, restore the current task, and only then rethrow the first recorded exception (`Evaluator.java:239-283`, `:336-362`). So **a group always waits for every arm, also when one arm throws or aborts**. That is the specification's fork-join rule (§4).
- **Throttle.** Arguments and tuples fork only while `getSurplusQueuedTaskCount() <= 3` (`TupleTask.java:119-121`, `Evaluator.java:342`). `forDo` has no such check.
- **`spawn`.** Each `spawn` makes a new one-thread pool (`interpreter/glue/prim/Thread.java:55-56`). `val()` and `wait()` busy-spin on a volatile flag (`SpawnTask.java:56-68`). A spawned task has no parent transaction (`SpawnTask` calls `super()`), so a `spawn` inside `atomic` runs outside the transaction. The specification forbids `spawn` inside `atomic` (`spawn.tex:28-31`), and nothing checks it. Row 938 is the spinning on an abrupt end.

### 1.2 Walk: the STM (`interpreter/evaluator/transactions/`, `interpreter/env/ReferenceCell.java`, `ValueNode.java`)

**Shape.** It descends from DSTM. Every mutable variable, mutable field and array element is a `ReferenceCell`. `AtomicArray` is one cell per element (`AtomicArray.java:26-37`). A cell holds a chain of `ValueNode`s, each with a value, a writer transaction, a set of readers and the older node (`ValueNode.java:23-34`). A transaction is a status in an `AtomicReference`: ACTIVE, COMMITTED, ABORTED or ORPHANED (`Transaction.java:36-46`).

- **Commit** is one compare-and-set from ACTIVE to COMMITTED (`Transaction.java:229-260`). A cell's `cleanup()` then reads a committed writer's node as the value, or as the value of the parent transaction for a nested commit. It pops an aborted writer's node (`ReferenceCell.java:87-121`). This is DSTM's "locator" scheme: the value is decided by the owner's status.
- **Readers are visible, and conflicts are detected eagerly.**
  - A transactional read registers the transaction in the node's read set, a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` (`ValueNode.java:66-72`, `ReadSet.java:68-84`).
  - A transactional write first resolves conflicts with every active reader that is not an ancestor, and with the writer (`ValueNode.java:95-116`). It then pushes a new node (`ReferenceCell.java:151-153`).
  - So validation at commit is only a status check (`BaseTask.java:91-100`).
- **Strong atomicity.** Plain access outside `atomic` is isolated from transactions. A non-transactional read aborts any active writer of the cell (`ReferenceCell.java:166-171`). A non-transactional write aborts every reader and writer (`:134-140`). The team added this in "Fixes for atomic/non-atomic interactions" (1d6d275bb, chf, 2008-02-13).
- **Nesting.** Nesting is closed. A nested `atomic` creates `new Transaction(parent)` (`tasks/BaseTask.java:105-121`), and an abort orphans its children (`Transaction.java:267-307`).
- **Contention manager and retries.** `GreedyManager` is wired in (`FortressTaskRunner.java:26`). Despite its name, it **always aborts the other transaction** (`GreedyManager.java:32-49`). Retries are unbounded and have no backoff (`FortressTaskRunner.java:147-175`).
- **`tryatomic`** runs the body once (`Evaluator.java:205-232`). Inside a transaction it is flattened into plain code (`:211-214`), which is defect N6 (§7).
- **Cost outside `atomic`.** Every cell access takes the cell's monitor and consults the transaction, and a write allocates a node, a `ReadSet` and a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` (`c4-parallelism.md` §6). The measured share was 0.8 % of allocation samples in a four-thread C4 run, not the bottleneck (`c4-parallelism.md`, "Measured, 2026-09-19").

### 1.3 Compiled: tasks and the pool (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`, `FortressTaskRunner*`, `FortressExecutable.java`)

- **Pool and tasks.** The pool is again a `ForkJoinPool` (`FortressTaskRunnerGroup.java:33`), sized by `FORTRESS_THREADS`, or half the CPUs when unset (`FortressExecutable.java:37-45`). A generated task class per arm extends `BaseTask`, whose constructor copies the parent's transaction (`BaseTask.java:83-86`).
- **Forking.** `forkIfProfitable` forks while the surplus queue is at most `spawnThreshold`, 5 by default (`:113-144`). `joinOrRun` runs an unforked task inline, and joins a forked one with the current task saved and restored (`:146-178`).
- **Arms.** `genParallelExprs` forks arms n-1 down to 1, runs arm 0 in place, then joins left to right (`CodeGen.java:1635-1712`). It does so only on the normal path: there is no handler that joins the remaining arms when one throws. That is defect N1.
- **Tuples and operators** fork only where `ParallelismAnalyzer` marked the node "worthy" (`CodeGen.java:5233-5236`).
- **Call arguments are evaluated in order** (`CodeGen.evalArg`, `:6935-6955`, under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???" at `:6939`). That is defect N5.

### 1.4 Compiled: the STM (`runtimeSystem/Transaction.java`)

**Shape.** This is a different algorithm: one global sequence lock, buffered writes and value-based validation. In form it is NOrec (Dalessandro, Spear and Scott, PPoPP 2010), though the code cites no paper.

- **The lock.** `global_lock` is an `AtomicInteger`; an odd value means a commit is writing back (`Transaction.java:76`, `:120-158`). Each transaction keeps a `snapshot` of it.
- **Reads.** A read takes the committed value. While the snapshot differs from the lock, it revalidates every recorded read by value and reads again. It then returns an own or ancestral write if there is one, and records the read (`:212-231`).
- **Writes** go to a private `Hashtable` (`:287-297`).
- **Commit.**
  - A read-only transaction returns at once (`:301`).
  - Otherwise the commit takes the lock by compare-and-set from its snapshot, revalidating whenever that fails (`:306-310`).
  - A top-level commit writes back, and a nested commit merges its reads and writes into its parent (`:312-344`, with the team's "This is subtle" comment at `:328`).
  - It releases the lock to the next even value (`:346`).
- **Conflict policy.** The committer wins; there is no contention manager. The generated handler retries without bound and calls `delayTransaction` (`CodeGen.java:1774-1802`). That backs off only when `FORTRESS_EXP_BACKOFF` is set; its default is off, "no evidence that it helps" (`FortressExecutable.java:33`, `BaseTask.java:214-230`).
- **Non-transactional access** is a plain volatile read or write of the cell (`MutableFValue.java:18-29`). Generated code chooses between the two at every access by calling `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`VarCodeGen.java:326-362`, `:483-546`; row 641). So **atomicity is weak**: plain accesses neither take nor check the lock (defect N2).
- `TransactionRecord.java` is an unused placeholder: `TXAbort` throws "Placeholder for now" (`:34-36`).

### 1.5 Compiled: arrays inside transactions (`compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java`, batch 28)

- **The `Object[]` store.** Inside a transaction, `get` and `put` go to `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`, keyed by the array and the index (`FortressArrayStore.java:45-57`, `Transaction.java:31-62`). Outside one, they are `VarHandle` volatile accesses. `init` is a compare-and-set from null outside a transaction, and a transactional read-then-write inside one (`:60-66`).
- **The `double[]` store** (`FortressRR64ArrayStore.java`) "takes no part in a transaction" (its header comment).
- **The prelude's `ZZ32Vector`** is a plain `int[]` with no transaction check (`FZZ32Vector.java:18`, `simpleIntVector.java:26-29`). That is defect N8.

### 1.6 The code generator's `atomic`

`forAtomicBlock` registers its exception-table entry before it emits the body (`CodeGen.java:1783`), so an outer block's handler precedes an inner one's (rows 934, 937; row 888 is the same for `try`). Its other gaps:

- It catches only `TransactionAbortException` (`:1780`), so a Fortress exception leaves the transaction pushed (row 324).
- It has no case for `AtomicExpr` or `TryAtomicExpr` (rows 875, 353).
- Mutable fields bypass the transaction (`VarCodeGen.java:209`, `:220`; row 319).

### 1.7 `ParallelismAnalyzer`

It is a syntactic heuristic: a node is worthy when at least `ARG_THRESHOLD = 2` of its operands are "compute intensive" (`ParallelismAnalyzer.java:44`, `:113-118`). Its defects:

- Every named function is added as compute intensive (`:218`), but the removal targets the `FnDecl` node, not the name (`:225`). So every named call counts.
- Calls whose text contains `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` or `println` are skipped (`:199-203`, with the team's comment "Is this right? The builtins could be intensive too, no?" at `:194`).
- "TODO: I don't think this handles mutual recursion" (`:40`).

### 1.8 Library: ranges, generators, reductions, `parloop`

- **The one library's parallel range.** `loop` splits at a power-of-two boundary into `do … also do … end`, down to single elements, with no grain size. `generate` joins the halves as a call's arguments, `red.join(loop'(lo,mid-1), loop'(mid,hi))` (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1308-1342`, `:1320`). The split depends only on `(lo, hi)`, so the join tree is deterministic (`c4-parallelism.md` §4).
- **`GeneratorLibrary.fss`** only composes generators; it has no `also` of its own.
- **Reductions** carry their algebra as objects: `join` and `empty`, with associativity assumed and checked nowhere (`FortressLibrary.fss:3412`; `c4-parallelism.md` §4).
- **`Matrix.mul`** splits rows and columns with `also` and runs the contraction axis in sequence, with the team's comment "If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition" (`FortressLibrary.fss:3046`). A second comment says the cache-oblivious product was dropped "due to lack of support for atomic increment of matrix elements" (`:3175-3177`). That text dates to 2008 at least (moved by jmaessen's library reorganization 1d2680d4d, 2008-03-24).
- **The compiler prelude.** `parloop` halves at the midpoint while the chunk is above `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK`, default 1 (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:357-369`). `gen` passes its halves as call arguments, and `seqgen` binds them as statements (`:381-414`). On the compiled path the two run alike (N5).

**Contention and abort policy, side by side**

| | walk | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| detection | eager: at the conflicting read or write, through visible readers | lazy: at validation, by value, when the global lock has moved |
| who wins | `GreedyManager`: always aborts the other | the first to commit |
| retry | `doIt`, unbounded, no backoff | generated handler, unbounded; backoff off by default |
| plain access beside `atomic` | aborts the conflicting transaction (strong) | not isolated (weak, N2) |
| nesting | closed; abort orphans the children | closed; a nested commit merges into the parent under the global lock |
| threads inside a block | share the block's transaction | share the block's transaction (unsafely, N3) |

## 2. Provenance

**Walk's STM began as Sun Labs' DSTM2 and became the team's own.**
- Christine Flood (`chf`) imported DSTM2 into the tree on 2007-06-13: "More Transactional Memory support. DSTM2 is now included in our source tree" (9aed945d8, 56 `dstm2/` paths). `ProjectFortress/src/dstm2/Transaction.java` there carries "Copyright 2006 Sun Microsystems" (`git show 9aed945d8:ProjectFortress/src/dstm2/Transaction.java`).

229	  - (c) The specification's shared and local objects (`shared-local.tex`), so that only shared objects pay.

233	  - (a) The code generator forks call arguments by `ParallelismAnalyzer`, as it does tuples.

239	## For FACTS
240	
241	1. **Walk's STM descends from DSTM2 and is strongly atomic.** It has visible readers, eager conflict detection, and a manager that always aborts the other transaction, chosen for work stealing.
242	   - For the work: walk is the reference for the specification's semantics of `atomic`.
243	   - Check: `git show 9aed945d8:ProjectFortress/src/dstm2/manager/GreedyManager.java` against `GreedyManager.java:22-49`; `WStrongAtomicity` printed 0 of 300.
244	   - Detail: §§1.2, 2.
245	2. **The compiled STM is in NOrec's form: one global sequence lock, buffered writes, value validation, closed nesting.** Flood wrote it in April–May 2012.
246	   - For the work: its commits do not scale; a contended counter is slower at four threads than at one.
247	   - Numbers: about 210 ns per uncontended block against 15 ns plain; 351–602 against 225–335 ns per contended update.
248	   - Check: `runcost.sh` (§3.3). Detail: §§1.4, 2, 3.3.

255	   - Check: `java/probe/ReadSetThreads.java`. Detail: §2.
256	
257	## Commands worked out
258	
259	- **Real commits of a file.** The phantom snapshot roots must be skipped. `authors.sh` in the scratchpad lists `git log --follow --format='%H|%P|…' a874948ac -- FILE` and drops parentless commits and commits touching more than 400 files.
260	- **Java probes against a tree's runtime.** `CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1); javac -cp "$CP" -d classes probe/*.java; java -cp "classes:$CP" probe.X`, from the tree's root with `FORTRESS_HOME` set.
261	- **Retry counts.** `FORTRESS_THREAD_STATISTICS=y bin/fortress run P` prints the pool and "Had to retry a transaction N times" at the end; N is a lower bound (§3.3).
262	
263	## Summary for the curator
264	
265	You asked whether Fortress's parallel foundation is firm. It is firm where microGPT stands, and soft where it does not stand yet.
266	
267	**Fork/join** is the core. A *task* is a piece of work. *Forking* hands it to the pool of worker threads, and *joining* waits for it. *Work stealing* means an idle thread takes queued tasks from a busy one. Both paths use Java's `ForkJoinPool`, and on private work it scales: 2.0–2.7× on four threads. Walk's tasks are sound. The compiled tasks have one structural fault that matters for microGPT: when one arm of a parallel block throws, the block exits without waiting for the others, which keep writing (N1). Compiled reductions such as `SUM` also run one body at a time, because the code generator evaluates a call's arguments in order (N5).
268	
269	**STM** (software transactional memory) runs an `atomic` block as a *transaction*. Its reads and writes take effect all at once, at *commit*, or are thrown away and the block *retried*, if another thread *conflicts*, that is, touches the same data. Fortress has two STMs.
270	
271	- **Walk's** grew from Sun Labs' own DSTM2 library (2006–2008). It records readers on each variable, so a conflicting writer can *abort* them at once. Plain reads and writes outside `atomic` also abort conflicting transactions. That is *strong atomicity*, which the specification requires. Its *contention manager*, the rule that picks who loses a conflict, always aborts the other side; the team removed DSTM2's waiting on purpose, writing that waiting interacts badly with work stealing. It passed every probe but one: `tryatomic` nested inside `atomic`.
272	- **The compiled one** was written in spring 2012, months before the project stopped. It keeps writes private until commit, takes one global lock to commit, and *validates* by checking that values it read are unchanged. That is a known good published design, NOrec. Its implementation is young. It aborts blocks that read their own writes (row 933). Its nested blocks can see half-made states, which breaks *opacity*, the promise that even a doomed transaction sees a consistent world (N4). It crashes when parallel tasks inside one block validate at once (N3). Plain writes slip past it, so its atomicity is *weak* (N2). Contended counters run slower on four threads than on one. In Java memory model terms (the rules on when one thread's write is visible to another, through *volatile*, locks and *compare-and-set*), its lock protocol is right; the faults are shared state assumed private.
273	
274	**Are fork/join and STM compatible?** Yes. The specification defines tasks inside a transaction coherently: they share it and synchronize through nested `atomic`. Research systems built exactly this a few years later and found it hard. The faults found are immature implementation, not a broken design. The design's costs are strong atomicity, parallel nesting, and a discipline that nothing checks.

content.content:
1	(* MicroGptFlat -- microGPT in native Fortress arrays, data designed after Hsu
     2	   (Run C4, the synthesis of rounds two and three: explorations/run-c4/design.md).
     3	   The model only: hyperparameters, the layout table, the four vector
     4	   functions, the step, Adam and the training loop, line for line against
     5	   explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_concise.dyalog and the formulas
     6	   (the tour: explorations/run-c4/tour.md).  The array vocabulary is FlatArrays,
     7	   the loaders and the corpus FlatData.  Run from explorations/run-c4/src: the
     8	   paths are relative. *)
     9	component MicroGptFlat
    10	export MicroGptFlat
    11	export Executable
    12	import FlatArrays.{...}
    13	import FlatData.{...}
    14	import System.{...}
    15	
    16	(* --------------------------------------------------- hyperparameters ---- *)
    17	(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)
    18	(epsilon, lr0, beta1, beta2, epsilon_A, nSteps) = (10.0^(-5), 0.01, 0.85, 0.99, 10.0^(-8), 1000)
    19	(corpusPath, weightsDir) = ("../../apl/reference/dzaima/docs.txt", "../../apl/reference/dzaima/w")
    20	
    21	(* -------------------------------------- rmsn, sm and their backward ------ *)
    22	rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|)
    23	sm(z: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do e = exp(z - (BIG MAX z)); e / (∑ e) end
    24	mask: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = mat(blockSize, blockSize, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if j > i then -(10.0^10) else 0.0 end)
    25	rmsn_b(dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
    26	    r = SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|); y = x / r
    27	    (dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r
    28	  end
    29	sm_b(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = p × (dy - (p DOT dy))
    30	
    31	(* ------------------------------- tactic 2/8: one vector, nine views ------ *)
    32	matName(i: ZZ32): String =
    33	    if i = 0 then "wte" elif i = 1 then "wpe" elif i = 2 then "lm_head" elif i = 3 then "attn_wq" elif i = 4 then "attn_wk"
    34	    elif i = 5 then "attn_wv" elif i = 6 then "attn_wo" elif i = 7 then "mlp_fc1" else "mlp_fc2" end
    35	matShape(i: ZZ32): (ZZ32, ZZ32) =
    36	    if (i = 0) OR (i = 2) then (vocabSize, nEmbd) elif i = 7 then (4 nEmbd, nEmbd) elif i = 8 then (nEmbd, 4 nEmbd) else (nEmbd, nEmbd) end
    37	matCount(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r, c) = matShape(i); r c end
    38	matOffset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = ∑[j <- 0#i] matCount(j)
    39	nParams(): ZZ32 = matOffset(9)
    40	view(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do (r, c) = matShape(i); view(p, matOffset(i), r, c) end
    41	
    42	(* -------------------- tactic 3/5: the corpus as one padded integer matrix - *)
    43	corpus: Corpus = loadCorpus(corpusPath, blockSize, bosId)
    44	
    45	(* ------------------------- the step: keys -> (loss, flat gradient). Pure. -- *)
    46	step(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): (RR64, Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    47	    ids = corpus.tokens(b, 0); tg = corpus.tokens(b, 1); vm = corpus.valid(b); nv = ∑ vm; pos = corpus.positions(b)
    48	    (wte, wpe, lm, wq, wk, wv, wo, f1, f2) = (view(p, 0), view(p, 1), view(p, 2), view(p, 3), view(p, 4), view(p, 5), view(p, 6), view(p, 7), view(p, 8))
    49	    h(m: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = heads(m, blockSize, nHead, headDim)
    50	    u(t: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = unheads(t, nHead)
    51	    (* -- forward, all (doc, pos) rows at once -- *)
    52	    x = gather(wte, ids) + gather(wpe, pos); xp = rows(rmsn, x); x1 = rows(rmsn, xp)
    53	    (q, k, v) = (x1 wq^T, x1 wk^T, x1 wv^T); (qh, kh, vh) = (h(q), h(k), h(v))
    54	    a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)
    55	    x2 = xp + hc wo^T; x3 = rows(rmsn, x2); m0 = x3 f1^T; mr = 0.0 MAX m0; x4 = x2 + mr f2^T
    56	    pr = rows(sm, x4 lm^T); loss = -(vm DOT log(pick(pr, tg))) / nv
    57	    (* -- backward, one line under each forward line, bottom-up -- *)
    58	    dL = diag(vm / nv) (pr - onehot(tg, vocabSize)); gLM = dL^T x4; dX4 = dL lm
    59	    gF2 = dX4^T mr; dM0 = (dX4 f2) × (m0 > 0.0); gF1 = dM0^T x3; dX3 = dM0 f1
    60	    dX2 = dX4 + rows(rmsn_b, dX3, x2); gWO = dX2^T hc; dh = h(dX2 wo)
    61	    dVh = a^T dh; dS = rows(sm_b, a, dh vh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)
    62	    dQh = dS kh; dKh = dS^T qh; (dQ, dK, dV) = (u(dQh), u(dKh), u(dVh))
    63	    (gWQ, gWK, gWV) = (dQ^T x1, dK^T x1, dV^T x1); dX1 = dQ wq + dK wk + dV wv
    64	    dXp = dX2 + rows(rmsn_b, dX1, xp); dX = rows(rmsn_b, dXp, x)
    65	    gWTE = (onehot(ids, vocabSize))^T dX; gWPE = (onehot(pos, blockSize))^T dX
    66	    (loss, flat(gWTE, gWPE, gLM, gWQ, gWK, gWV, gWO, gF1, gF2))
    67	  end
    68	
    69	(* --------------------- Adam: three whole-vector expressions over p, m, v -- *)
    70	adam(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], g: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: ZZ32, lr: RR64):
    71	    (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    72	    m' = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) g
    73	    v' = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (g × g)
    74	    p' = p - (lr (m' / (1 - beta1^t))) / (SQRT (v' / (1 - beta2^t)) + epsilon_A)
    75	    (p', m', v')
    76	  end
    77	learningRate(s: ZZ32): RR64 = lr0 (1 - (1.0 s) / nSteps)
    78	
    79	(* --------------------------------------------------- training ----------- *)
    80	run(): () = do
    81	    println "microgpt flat | params " nParams() " | corpus " corpus.size() " x " (blockSize + 1) " | batch 1, 5 steps"
    82	    bsz = 1
    83	    p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := loadParams(weightsDir, matName, 9, nParams())
    84	    m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
    85	    v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
    86	    for s <- seq(0#5) do
    87	        t0 = nanoTime()
    88	        (l, g) = step(p, keys(bsz, fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => (s bsz + i) MOD corpus.size()))
    89	        (p, m, v) := adam(p, m, v, g, s + 1, learningRate(s))
    90	        println "step " (s + 1) " loss " l "  (" ((nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000) " ms)"
    91	    end
    92	  end
    93	end

shiftLeft(amount: ZZ32): CompactFullScalarRange = bounded1Range(self.lower - amount, self.upper - amount)
    shiftRight(amount: ZZ32): CompactFullScalarRange (* ensures { |outcome| = |self| } *)
        =  bounded1Range(self.lower + amount, self.upper + amount)
end

object CompactFullParScalarRange(l:ZZ32, r:ZZ32)
        extends { CompactFullScalarRange }
    getter lower(): ZZ32 = l
    getter upper(): ZZ32 = r
    getter left(): Just[\ZZ32\] = Just[\ZZ32\](l)
    getter right(): Just[\ZZ32\] = Just[\ZZ32\](r)
    getter asDebugString(): String = "CompactFullParScalarRange(" l "," r ")"
    seq(self): CompactFullSeqScalarRange = CompactFullSeqScalarRange(l,r)
    generate[\T\](red:Reduction[\T\], body: ZZ32->T): T =
        if r < l then
            red.empty()
        else
            loop'(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): T =
                if lo=hi then
                    body(lo)
                elif 0 <= (hi DOTMINUS lo) < grainSize then
                    CompactFullSeqScalarRange(lo,hi).generate[\T\](red,body)
                else
                    (* Identify power-of-2 boundary in region, split there *)
                    split = partitionL((lo BITXOR hi) DOTPLUS 1)
                    mid   = hi BITAND (BITNOT (split DOTMINUS 1))
                    red.join(loop'(lo,mid-1),loop'(mid,hi))
                end
            loop'(l,r)
        end
    loop(body: ZZ32->()): () =
        if r < l then
            ()
        else
            lop(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): () =
                if lo=hi then
                    body(lo)
                elif 0 <= (hi DOTMINUS lo) < grainSize then
                    CompactFullSeqScalarRange(lo,hi).loop(body)
                else
                    (* Identify power-of-2 boundary in region, split there *)
                    split = partitionL((lo BITXOR hi) DOTPLUS 1)
                    mid   = hi BITAND (BITNOT (split DOTMINUS 1))
                    do
                        lop(lo,mid-1)
                    also do
                        lop(mid,hi)
                    end
                end
            lop(l,r)
        end


end
